analysis.one_liner: Restores full military retirement inflation adjustments paid for by taxing U.S.-managed foreign corporations.
analysis.headline: A bill with 24 cosponsors to reverse the 2013 cut in military retirees' cost-of-living adjustments died in the Senate Finance Committee without a markup or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have canceled one part of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2013: a permanent reduction in the annual inflation adjustment to retirement pay for service members who retired before age 62. To cover the cost, it would treat foreign corporations that are actually run from the United States, and that are publicly traded or hold $50 million or more in assets, as domestic companies for income-tax purposes, ending their ability to book profits abroad while being managed here.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired service members under age 62, who would get back the full annual cost-of-living adjustment to their retirement pay that the 2013 budget act reduced; over a career, that 1-percentage-point reduction compounds into a meaningful loss of retirement income.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 403 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2013, which reduced the cost-of-living adjustment to military retirement pay for retirees under age 62.

Pays for the restoration by treating foreign corporations whose management and control occurs primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for income-tax purposes, if their stock is regularly traded or their gross assets total $50 million or more.

The new tax rule reaches companies where executive decisions are made in the U.S. and investment funds whose investment decisions are made in the United States, even when the entity is incorporated abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign corporations that are managed primarily from the United States but incorporated abroad — including publicly traded companies and investment funds with $50 million or more in assets — would owe U.S. income tax as domestic corporations. The change takes effect two years after enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S.-managed foreign corporations and investment funds

drawbacks.text: The management-and-control test is complex: Treasury would have to write regulations defining when a company is 'primarily' managed in the U.S., and the standard reaches any corporation with $50 million or more in gross assets or assets under management, a threshold that could sweep in midsize firms and funds with only modest U.S. ties.
The restoration is not immediate: the new tax rule applies only to tax years beginning two years or more after enactment, so retirees would wait before their full adjustment returned.

The bill pays for one group's restored benefits with a tax increase rather than broader deficit reduction; the underlying COLA cut existed because the 2013 budget deal needed offsetting savings, and this bill simply moves that cost onto a different set of companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Restoring the full inflation adjustment for working-age military retirees is a substantial, concrete benefit to a group that earned those benefits through service, and the offset targets a widely criticized structure — companies and funds that operate out of the U.S. but book income as foreign entities. The main honest concerns are administrative: the $50 million threshold and the 'primarily managed' standard would need careful regulation, and the benefit phase-in is slow. On balance the trade is straightforward and the design problems are fixable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2013, sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there with no committee action of any kind until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on December 17, 2013, two days before the end of the first session, with 17 original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; it was the only action the bill ever received.
By the end of the 113th Congress the bill had 23 cosponsors — 21 Democrats and 2 independents — and no further committee or floor action, so it never received a markup or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S.-managed foreign corporations and investment funds kept being taxed as foreign entities, and working-age military retirees remained under the reduced cost-of-living formula from the 2013 budget act while the bill got no committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent (21 Democrats, 2 independents) and no Republican signed on, while the cost-of-living cut the bill would repeal came from a bipartisan budget agreement negotiated by both parties.

industries.note: Companies incorporated abroad but run from the United States would be treated as domestic for income tax, ending lower foreign-booked taxation. Their tax savings come at the expense of the U.S. Treasury, which this bill would redirect to military retirees.
Funds with $50 million or more in assets under management whose investment decisions are made in the United States would be treated as domestic corporations for tax, even if incorporated elsewhere.
Retirees under 62 continue to receive the reduced cost-of-living adjustment written into the 2013 budget act, since the bill that would have restored it never advanced.
